title: No pressure, no problem: Superconductor record shattered after 30 years
summary:
For over three decades, the world of superconductivity has been stuck. Since 1993, the highest temperature at which a material could carry electricity with zero resistance under normal atmospheric pressure was 133 Kelvin—a frigid -140°C. That record, held by a mercury-based ceramic, seemed unbreakable. Until now.

Researchers at the University of Houston, led by physics professor Ching-Wu Chu and assistant professor Liangzi Deng, have pushed the boundary to 151 Kelvin (-122°C). Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, their work represents an 18-degree leap—a huge step in a field where even single-digit gains are celebrated. "Transmitting electricity in the grid loses about 8% of the electricity," Chu explains. "If we conserve that energy, that's billions of dollars of savings and it also saves us lots of effort and reduces environmental impacts."

The secret to their success is a relatively new technique called pressure quenching. The team first subjected their material to intense pressure, which dramatically boosted its superconducting transition temperature (Tc). While still under pressure, they cooled it to a specific temperature, then suddenly released the pressure. Remarkably, the enhanced superconducting state remained stable. "Other researchers have shown that reaching superconductivity at room temperature under pressure is achievable," says Chu. "Our method shows that it is possible to retain that state without maintaining pressure." This is crucial because maintaining high pressure is impractical for real-world applications—think of it as trapping a genie in a bottle, then breaking the bottle but the genie stays put.

Superconductors are materials that conduct electricity without any energy loss. They're already used in MRI machines and particle accelerators, but their need for extreme cooling (often with liquid helium) makes them expensive and limits widespread use. A superconductor that works at higher temperatures, especially at ambient pressure, could revolutionize power grids, energy storage, quantum computing, and fusion energy. The new record is still far from room temperature (about 300 K), but it narrows the gap. Chu, who co-discovered the famous YBCO superconductor in 1987, sees this as a critical milestone. The pressure-quenching method could be applied to other materials, potentially unlocking even higher Tc values. For now, the team has given scientists a new tool to explore the quantum mysteries of superconductivity—and a tantalizing glimpse of a future where electricity flows without waste.
why_it_matters: If superconductors that work at normal pressure and higher temperatures become practical, the way we transmit and use electricity could be transformed—making energy cheaper, greener, and enabling technologies like quantum computers and fusion reactors in your lifetime.

background_read: Superconductivity was first discovered in 1911 in mercury cooled to near absolute zero. For decades, physicists dreamed of materials that could superconduct at higher temperatures, leading to the discovery of 'high-temperature' superconductors in the 1980s by researchers like Prof. Ching-Wu Chu (who co-discovered the famous YBCO superconductor in 1987 at the University of Houston, a public research university in Texas). The previous record at ambient pressure, 133 K, had stood since 1993, held by a mercury-based ceramic. Although scientists have reached room-temperature superconductivity under extreme pressures, those conditions are impractical. The new pressure-quenching method, detailed in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (a prestigious scientific journal), offers a path to stabilizing such states without continuous pressure, potentially bringing us closer to real-world applications like lossless power lines.

perspectives.description: The new record shows that a long-barrier can be broken, raising hope for superconductors that operate at everyday temperatures. If realized, lossless power grids could save billions and cut greenhouse gas emissions from transmission losses.

151 K is still extremely cold (−122°C), requiring cooling systems that are costly and complex. The pressure-quenching technique, while clever, may not work with all materials, and practical room-temperature superconductors remain a distant dream.

The pressure-quenching method is a new tool for scientists to study the quantum behavior of superconductors, independent of whether it leads directly to room-temperature devices. It builds on decades of incremental progress in high-pressure physics and materials science.

This achievement could spur attempts to apply pressure quenching to other promising materials, potentially unlocking even higher transition temperatures. The gap to room temperature is narrowing, and each advance teaches us more about the underlying physics, making the next breakthrough more likely.
